analyst:
North Carolina enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 24-8 overall and 12-6 in the ACC, good for fourth in the league, after finishing the regular season 24-7 and then losing 80-79 to Clemson in the ACC quarterfinals on March 12, 2026. ESPN’s team page lists UNC at 24-8 and 12-6 ACC, while Carolina’s own ACC Tournament notes listed the Tar Heels at 24-7, 12-6 before the Clemson loss. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/_/id/153/north-carolina-tar-heels))

Offensively, this is a Hubert Davis team that still plays with Carolina’s traditional paint-touch foundation but with much heavier perimeter volume than older UNC groups. UNC averaged 79.8 points per game, shot 47.3% from the field, made 34.5% from three, and averaged only 9.7 turnovers per game through 32 games. Carolina’s own game notes stated on December 1 that UNC was attempting 25.6 threes per game, a rate that would break the program record; by March 10, UNC’s notes also said Davis’ teams had produced four of the lowest turnover-per-game seasons in school history and a 1.57 assist-turnover ratio, second-best in UNC history. The practical result is a modernized secondary-break team: they still want early offense, rim runs and post seals for Henri Veesaar, but they are far more willing than vintage UNC teams to flow into drag screens, pitch-ahead threes and inside-out spacing around Caleb Wilson, Luka Bogavac and Derek Dixon. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/153))

Specific tendencies show up in their best wins. In the 67-64 road win at Kentucky on December 2, UNC won despite Kentucky shooting 43% to UNC’s 41% and despite the Wildcats holding UNC to only 30% from three; the difference was Carolina’s 41-30 rebounding edge and its ability to keep generating interior chances until Derek Dixon scored the tiebreaking layup with 16 seconds left. In the 77-74 win over Louisville on February 23, UNC used what its recap described as a 17-2 second-half spurt, scored 40-24 in the paint, and shot 53.6% overall. That is a good snapshot of the scheme: Davis wants the ball to the lane first, whether by post feed, straight-line drive or secondary action off a ball screen, and then lets kick-out shooting become the counter. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/game/_/gameId/401806365/north-carolina-kentucky))

The core offensive personnel defines the playbook. Freshman forward Caleb Wilson leads UNC in scoring at 19.8 points per game and also leads in rebounds at 9.4, steals at 1.5 and blocks at 1.4. Center Henri Veesaar gives them an interior target at 16.7 points and 8.7 rebounds while shooting 61.4% from the floor and 42.0% from three, which means Carolina can use him in both low-post seals and pick-and-pop actions. Seth Trimble is the slashing guard and late-clock attacker at 14.0 points per game, while Bogavac supplies wing shooting at 9.8 points with 52 made threes and Derek Dixon adds 47 made threes at 39.5%. Kyan Evans, despite only 4.1 points per game, is important as a table-setter with 2.6 assists. Those numbers point to a specific structure: Wilson and Veesaar are the first options, Trimble is the pressure-release creator, and Bogavac/Dixon are the spacing pieces around them. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/153))

Defensively, Carolina is more conservative than gambling. The numbers say 71.3 points allowed per game, 5.3 steals, 3.4 blocks, and again just 9.7 turnovers committed offensively, which fits Davis’ preference for possession control on both ends. UNC does not profile as a full-court havoc team; instead it tries to protect the paint with size, finish possessions on the glass, and make opponents score over length. When that structure holds, it looks like the 71-68 win over Duke on February 7, when Carolina held Duke to 68 points and survived despite trailing by 13 in the first half and 11 in the second. When the structure breaks, the losses are revealing. SMU scored 97 on January 3 while shooting 60% overall and 52% from three; NC State scored 82 on February 17 and won by 24, its biggest win over UNC since 1962 according to Carolina’s recap; Michigan State beat UNC 74-58 on November 27 while holding the Tar Heels to 38% shooting and 4-of-23 from three. Those games show the vulnerability: if opponents move Carolina’s bigs, spray the ball to shooters, or force the Tar Heels to defend multiple actions in sequence, the defense can give up efficient nights. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/153))

Hubert Davis’ coaching philosophy is visible in the statistical profile and in specific adjustment games. Carolina’s official notes credit his teams with historically low turnover rates and elite assist-turnover balance, so the offensive philosophy is clearly to create clean shots without wasting possessions. His in-game adjustment history this season is mixed but documented. Against Louisville on February 23, UNC trailed by 10 in the first half, then changed the game with a 17-2 run and a stronger paint attack to win 77-74. Against Duke on February 7, Davis stayed with his group despite trailing most of the night, and Carolina eventually stole the game on Seth Trimble’s three with 0.4 seconds left. But against top-end offense, his counters have not always solved the problem: at Duke on March 7, UNC opened the second half with two threes to cut the margin to 41-40, then got buried by a 24-2 Duke run; at NC State on February 17, the Tar Heels trailed by 16 at halftime and never meaningfully recovered. That pattern suggests Davis is effective at restoring offensive rhythm and late-game structure, but this team can still get overwhelmed by sustained shot-making and turnover pressure. ([goheels.com](https://goheels.com/news/2026/3/10/mens-basketball-mbb-heads-to-acc-tournament-as-no-4-seed?utm_source=openai))

Clutch execution is a real Carolina strength. The best example is February 7 against Duke: UNC won 71-68 on Seth Trimble’s right-corner three with 0.4 seconds left, and that shot gave Carolina its only lead of the game. On December 20 against Ohio State, UNC won 71-70 when Henri Veesaar dunked with 7.2 seconds left off a pass from a stumbling Trimble. On December 2 at Kentucky, Derek Dixon scored the tiebreaking layup with 16 seconds remaining in a 67-64 win. On March 3 against Clemson, Bogavac scored 17 second-half points and then hit two free throws with 12.2 seconds left to push the lead to three in a 67-63 win. Even the narrow 87-84 win over Wake Forest on January 10 matters here: UNC led for 97% of the game and survived a late push. The counterexample is the March 12 ACC quarterfinal loss to Clemson, 80-79, which shows the same roster can play coin-flip games in either direction. ([goheels.com](https://goheels.com/news/2026/2/7/mens-basketball-mbb-recap-vs-duke?utm_source=openai))

The key players are easy to define. Wilson is the centerpiece and the highest-upside tournament swing piece: 19.8 points, 9.4 rebounds, 57.8% shooting, plus 476 total points in 24 games. Carolina’s March 10 notes say he was averaging 19.8 and that despite missing seven games he had still scored more points than any other Tar Heel. His standout moment in a marquee win was 23 points in the February 7 upset of Duke. Veesaar is the efficiency anchor: 16.7 points, 8.7 rebounds, 61.4% FG, 42.0% from three, plus 25 points and nine rebounds in the 87-84 win over Wake Forest and 26 points against ETSU earlier in the year. Trimble is the emotional closer: 14.0 points per game, the game-winner against Duke, and a career-high 30 points with 11 made field goals in the February 23 win over Louisville. Bogavac is the microwave spacer: 9.8 points per game, season-high 20 against Clemson on March 3, including 17 in the second half. Dixon is the situational shot-maker: 6.4 points per game overall, but he delivered the winning layup at Kentucky and shoots 39.5% from three. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/153))

North Carolina’s best wins all revealed useful traits. The 67-64 win at Kentucky on December 2 showed road toughness and late-game poise. The 71-70 win over Ohio State on December 20 showed they can execute in the final possession. The 71-68 win over Duke on February 7 showed comeback ability against elite talent. The 77-74 win over Louisville on February 23 showed they can recover from a double-digit deficit and dominate the paint. The worst losses exposed the pressure points. Michigan State’s 74-58 win on November 27 showed UNC could be physically disrupted and forced into bad perimeter offense; the Tar Heels shot only 17% from three. SMU’s 97-83 win on January 3 showed the defense can be carved up by quick guards and hot shooting. NC State’s 82-58 win on February 17 showed how vulnerable Carolina becomes when it cannot stabilize the game early. Duke’s 76-61 win on March 7 showed that against a top-5 roster, turnover stretches can become knockout blows; Carolina’s own rapid-reaction piece noted Duke scored 24 points off turnovers, a season high by a UNC opponent. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/game/_/gameId/401806365/north-carolina-kentucky))

As for Hubert Davis’ NCAA Tournament history as head coach, Carolina’s official materials list him at 8-3 in NCAA Tournament play entering the 2026 field. That run includes the 2022 national title game appearance, a 2023 second-round exit, and a 2025 tournament in which UNC won a First Four game over San Diego State before losing in the round of 64 to Ole Miss. In round terms by season: 2022 reached the national championship game; 2023 reached the second round; 2024 missed the tournament; 2025 reached the round of 64 after advancing through the First Four. ([goheels.com](https://goheels.com/news/2026/3/11/mens-basketball-mbb-heads-to-acc-tournament-as-no-4-seed?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: this is a dangerous but not invulnerable Carolina team. The traditional-analyst view is simple. UNC has NCAA-level frontline talent in Wilson and Veesaar, enough shooting to punish help, and proven late-game shot making from Trimble, Bogavac and Dixon. But the Tar Heels are not a lockdown defense, and the losses to SMU, NC State, Clemson and Duke show they can be pushed off script by teams that spread them out, pressure their guards, and score efficiently for long stretches. If the game is close late, Carolina has repeatedly shown it can win it. If the opponent turns it into a pace-and-space shootout or a turnover avalanche, UNC becomes far more ordinary. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/153))
forecaster:
North Carolina enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament profile range as a strong but slightly polarizing team: good enough in predictive systems to look like a dangerous second-weekend threat, but not so dominant on the résumé side that every metric fully agrees. As of March 2026, the Tar Heels are 24-8 overall and 12-6 in the ACC, with a 12-1 Division I non-conference record, a NET ranking of 24, a BPI ranking of 30, a KenPom/Pomeroy ranking of 29, and a Bart Torvik T-Rank of 27. Their result-based résumé is somewhat better than their pure predictive profile: Warren Nolan lists UNC at KPI 16, SOR 21, and WAB 21, which suggests the team has accumulated enough quality wins to outperform its underlying power numbers by a modest amount. They are 6-8 in Quadrant 1, 5-0 in Quadrant 2, 8-0 in Quadrant 3, and 5-0 in Quadrant 4, which is a clean profile outside top-tier games but not the résumé of a team that has consistently beaten elite opposition. ([ncaa.com](https://www.ncaa.com/rankings/basketball-men/d1/ncaa-mens-basketball-net-rankings))

The best hard efficiency snapshot available from broadly accessible public sources comes via Bart Torvik’s team page snapshot, which shows North Carolina with an adjusted offensive efficiency of 120.8 points per 100 possessions and an adjusted defensive efficiency of 91.7. That combination implies a roughly +29.1 adjusted efficiency margin, squarely in the national top tier by tournament standards even if not in the absolute inner circle. Torvik’s archived page also shows UNC’s offensive eFG% at 51.6, offensive turnover rate at 18.2, offensive rebounding rate at 40.0, and free-throw rate at 35.2; defensively, the Heels are allowing a 45.4 eFG%, forcing turnovers on 17.7% of possessions, allowing a 31.2 offensive rebounding rate, and conceding a 37.8 free-throw rate. Those numbers paint a very clear stylistic identity: this is a team that wins first with shot suppression and rebounding dominance, not with hyper-aggressive turnover creation. ([barttorvik.com](https://barttorvik.com/2015/North%20Carolina.html))

The most striking single stat in that Torvik snapshot is the offensive rebounding rate. At 40.0%, North Carolina ranks fifth nationally in that capture, which is an elite extra-possession figure and one that aligns with UNC’s traditional frontcourt-heavy identity. Just as important, the same source shows the Tar Heels with a 3-point attempt rate of only 22.3, ranked 350th nationally. That is extremely low in the modern game and confirms that this offense is not perimeter-volume driven. UNC is generating offense primarily through interior scoring, offensive rebounds, and free-throw pressure rather than by bombing away from three. Their 3-point percentage in that snapshot is 35.8%, solid but not overwhelming, so the profile is not “great shooting team”; it is “selective three-point team.” ([barttorvik.com](https://barttorvik.com/2015/North%20Carolina.html))

UNC’s schedule profile is respectable but not overwhelming. Their NET strength of schedule is 35 and non-conference NET SOS is 95; Warren Nolan also lists their RPI SOS at 11 and non-conference RPI SOS at 37. In plain terms, the overall schedule has enough weight to validate the résumé, but the non-conference build was more opportunistic than punishing. That matters when interpreting the 24-8 record: it is real and valuable, but the predictive systems are signaling that the win-loss mark may slightly flatter the team relative to true top-10 caliber dominance. The 6-8 Quadrant 1 record reinforces that read. UNC has proven it belongs, but it has not consistently crushed its best competition. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=North-Carolina))

Recent-form data is actually encouraging. Torvik’s available “Last 10 Eff.” snapshot shows North Carolina at 124.4 adjusted offensive efficiency and 91.3 adjusted defensive efficiency over the last 10 games, with a Barthag of .9596 and a national rank of 7 in that form window. Even allowing for the possibility that public snapshots lag or represent a moment-in-time capture, the directional message is important: UNC’s recent 10-game efficiency level has looked stronger than its full-season ranking. In other words, this is not a team limping into March by the numbers. The offense, especially, appears to have sharpened late. ([barttorvik.com](https://barttorvik.com/2015/North%20Carolina.html))

That trend helps explain one of the central divergences between the eye test and the spreadsheet. Conventional wisdom may see North Carolina as somewhat old-school, interior-oriented, maybe even a bit clunky because of the low three-point volume. But the data says that stylistic conservatism has not prevented high-end efficiency. A 120.8 adjusted offense is excellent, and a last-10 offensive figure of 124.4 is even better. The offense does not need huge three-point volume because it recovers misses, gets to the line at a decent rate, and converts efficiently enough inside the arc to maintain elite scoring efficiency. At the same time, the defensive profile is a little less disruptive than some fans might assume. Forcing turnovers on only 17.7% of possessions is not a chaos defense; it is more of a positional, contest-and-clean-the-glass unit. ([barttorvik.com](https://barttorvik.com/2015/North%20Carolina.html))

There is also a subtle warning sign in the profile: free-throw dynamics. UNC’s own free-throw rate is healthy at 35.2, but defensively it allows a 37.8 FTR in the Torvik snapshot, which is on the loose side for a contender. If there is a vulnerability that can surface in tournament settings, it is that opponents may be able to stabilize possessions at the stripe rather than getting completely erased in the half court. That issue is partly offset by strong defensive shot suppression, but against elite whistle-drawing teams it is the kind of flaw that can swing a toss-up game. ([barttorvik.com](https://barttorvik.com/2015/North%20Carolina.html))

Putting it all together, North Carolina’s 2026 tournament case is that of a team with top-30 consensus predictive standing, top-25 NET standing, elite offensive rebounding, very low 3-point dependence, and a defense that is better at controlling quality than creating havoc. The résumé says solidly in the field and dangerous; the predictive numbers say clearly good, though not quite a national-title favorite; the recent-form indicators suggest the Heels may be peaking at the right time. The biggest gap between public perception and reality is probably on offense: this is not just a “tough, physical UNC team,” but a genuinely efficient one. The biggest gap in the other direction is that the résumé and brand might suggest a more dominant power than the underlying top-25-to-top-30 metrics actually show. On balance, the numbers describe a team that is highly capable of winning multiple NCAA Tournament games if it can continue to own the glass and avoid being dragged into a foul-heavy or three-point-variance-driven game script. ([ncaa.com](https://www.ncaa.com/rankings/basketball-men/d1/ncaa-mens-basketball-net-rankings))
matchup-analyst:
North Carolina enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as an offense-first team that is built around two elite interior scorers, Caleb Wilson and Henri Veesaar, but with a perimeter volume profile that can swing games hard in either direction. Through 32 games, UNC averaged 79.78 points, shot 47.3% from the floor, took 801 threes in 32 games (25.0 attempts per game), and got 19.8 points/9.4 rebounds from Wilson plus 16.7 points/8.7 rebounds from Veesaar. Veesaar also shot 42.0% from three on 37-of-88, which means Carolina can play true 5-out spacing with a 7-footer who must be honored above the break. Luka Bogavac (52 threes), Derek Dixon (47), Jonathan Powell (38), and Kyan Evans (32) give Hubert Davis four other perimeter shooters, but several are streaky: Bogavac shot 35.9%, Powell 38.4%, Dixon 39.5%, while Evans was only 30.5%. ([goheels.com](https://goheels.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

Style-of-play diagnosis: UNC wants to score through paint touches that trigger kick-out threes, not through pure guard creation. The statistical tell is roster construction: Wilson and Veesaar combined for 994 points and 486 rebounds, and UNC’s top two scorers are both frontcourt players, while the guards are more secondary finishers than dominant on-ball engines. Their offense is most dangerous when Veesaar spaces a rim protector out, Wilson attacks a rotating defense, and Trimble slashes off the catch. The tactics that disrupt this are: 1) switching size onto Wilson so he sees bodies early, 2) top-locking shooters and forcing UNC into late-clock self-creation, and 3) winning the defensive glass so Carolina’s frontcourt scoring does not produce second chances. Duke’s 76-61 win on March 7 is the clearest template: after UNC cut it to 47-44, Duke ripped off a 16-0 run, and the Tar Heels “went six minutes without a point and managed one basket over more than 10 minutes.” That is what UNC looks like when the first action is denied and the game becomes one-on-one creation instead of flow offense. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/401820788))

Press vulnerability: UNC’s season-long turnover numbers are good on the surface, but pressure has still bothered specific lineups, especially when one of the frontcourt hubs is missing. NC State’s 82-58 win on February 17 is the best evidence. Quadir Copeland posted 20 points, seven assists, four steals, and zero turnovers, and UNC “struggled to get into its offensive rhythm and get good shots early.” The Tar Heels finished at 31.7% from the field, missed 17 of their first 18 threes, and committed 12 turnovers. That game matters because it shows what happens when a pressure guard disrupts entry flow and Carolina is forced into bailout threes instead of paint creation. NC State’s guard activity clearly sped UNC up without letting them play fast on their own terms. ([goheels.com](https://goheels.com/news/2026/2/17/mens-basketball-mbb-recap-at-ncsu))

Zone vulnerability: the cleanest practical read is that UNC can shoot its way out of zone looks, but only if the ball gets inside-out first; if the opponent keeps them perimeter-oriented, the offense bogs down. In the March 3 win over Clemson, UNC made 12 threes and won 67-63 despite trailing 30-27 at halftime, and the staff notes that in the second half Carolina shot 60.7% from the floor while allowing only two points off turnovers. That suggests effective halftime counters versus a defense that had controlled the first half. The opposite outcome came at NC State, where UNC had no interior stabilizer with Wilson and Veesaar out and resorted to 33 threes, making only five. So the specific anti-UNC tactic is not simply “play zone”; it is “play a compact zone or gap help behind size and force non-paint threes from lineups without both stars.” ([goheels.com](https://goheels.com/news/2026/3/3/mens-basketball-unc-clemson-postgame-notes?utm_source=openai))

Preferred pace: Carolina prefers a game where possessions are not chaotic but where they can run opportunistically off stops and rebounds. Their offense is too frontcourt-skilled to be purely grind-it-out, yet too dependent on structure to thrive in random, turnover-heavy games. Evidence: in comeback wins over Kansas, Virginia, Duke, and Clemson, UNC repeatedly won after halftime by re-establishing offensive structure rather than by winning a track meet. Against Kansas, UNC scored 58 second-half points and shot 24-of-36 (66.7%) after trailing 37-29 at the half. Against Virginia, they erased a 16-point deficit and outscored the Cavaliers 58-37 over the final 22:05. Those are not frantic, random runs; those are half-court execution stretches. To force the opposite, opponents should extend pressure after makes, flatten the game into guard initiation, and attack early in transition before UNC can load its help behind Veesaar/Wilson. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/story/_/id/46888624/north-carolina-rallies-makes-early-statement-topping-kansas))

Size/athleticism mismatches by position: PG/lead guard is the clearest UNC vulnerability because there is no dominant big-minute creator; Kyan Evans is 4.1 points per game, Derek Dixon 6.4, and neither profiles as a downhill star. Opponents with a big scoring point guard can tilt the game, as NC State got from Copeland. At the 2, Seth Trimble gives UNC athleticism and point-of-attack defense, but his offensive value is slashing-based, so long defenders can shrink him. On the wing, Bogavac is a shooter first; physical wings can target him off the bounce. At the 4, Caleb Wilson is the mismatch weapon for UNC: 19.8 points and 9.4 rebounds with 57.8% shooting. If an opponent has a true 6-8/6-9 athlete who can absorb him without extra help, that changes the game. At the 5, Veesaar is the swing piece: 16.7 points, 8.7 rebounds, 61.4% FG, 42.0% from three, 37 blocks. Teams with a mobile rim protector who can contest him inside and still close to the arc are best equipped. Duke’s Cameron Boozer line in the March 7 game — 26 points, 15 rebounds, five assists — also showed UNC can be hurt by elite opposing frontcourt size and skill. ([goheels.com](https://goheels.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

Isolation vs team offense tendencies: UNC is much more team-offense than isolation-offense. The evidence is assist distribution and scoring spread. Carolina had 511 assists on 896 made field goals, an assist rate of roughly 57.0%, which is strong evidence of a pass-driven offense. Individually, Bogavac had 71 assists, Dixon 84, Evans 82, Trimble 65, Wilson 64, and Veesaar 60; no one player dominates the creation burden. That means the offense is built around shared creation and advantage passing, not repeated empty-side isolations. When opponents blow up the first action, UNC does not have a 25%-usage heliocentric guard to rescue possessions late. ([goheels.com](https://goheels.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

Transition offense and defense frequency: publicly available UNC sources do not provide full Synergy-style possession frequency splits for transition offense/defense, so the best verified tournament-facing read comes from game evidence and scoring profile rather than an unsupported percentage guess. Carolina becomes more dangerous in transition when Wilson and Trimble can attack unsettled defenders; it becomes less effective when forced into half-court jump shooting without paint collapse. Defensively, their biggest transition issue is matching size early and protecting the rim-to-trailer three sequence. Duke’s second-half avalanche and NC State’s early shotmaking both came from UNC losing control of game rhythm before the defense could get set. Because exact frequency percentages were not available in the fetched primary sources, I will not fabricate them. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/401820788))

Coaching adaptability: this is a real UNC strength. Carolina is explicitly documented as 4-5 when trailing at halftime, with comeback wins over Kansas, Virginia, Duke, and Clemson. That matters because those are not low-major escapes; those are quality-opponent adjustment wins. Against Kansas, UNC turned a 37-29 halftime deficit into an 87-74 win by scoring 58 in the second half; Bill Self said the game “got away from us” in the first five minutes after halftime. Against Virginia, UNC rallied from 16 down for an 85-80 road win. Against Clemson, UNC trailed 30-27 at half and then shot 60.7% in the second half. Those are direct pieces of evidence that Hubert Davis and staff do make effective midgame adjustments. ([goheels.com](https://goheels.com/news/2026/3/3/mens-basketball-unc-clemson-postgame-notes?utm_source=openai))

Concrete game plan: To beat North Carolina you must crowd Wilson with a like-sized athlete, use a mobile 5 on Veesaar, and make UNC win with secondary guards creating off the dribble. Pick up Evans/Dixon early to chew clock, top-lock Bogavac and Powell off movement, and switch enough to keep the ball from entering the paint comfortably. On offense, drag Veesaar into space in ball screens, force Wilson to defend multiple actions, and attack before UNC’s half-court help is organized. Most important: finish possessions with defensive rebounds. If Carolina gets clean defensive boards, they can flow into early offense and let Wilson/Trimble attack scrambled matchups. If you control the glass, flatten their pace, and force 25+ three-point attempts from the non-star perimeter players, the evidence from Duke’s 76-61 win and NC State’s 82-58 win says UNC becomes beatable. ([goheels.com](https://goheels.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))
